newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Freeze sought on more Mobutu assets, Swiss ponder.
newsitem.headline: Freeze sought on more Mobutu assets, Swiss ponder.

text.p: Zairean rebels' efforts to block President Mobutu Sese Seko's wealth gathered pace on Thursday as Switzerland studied the legitimacy of a Zairean request to seize his fortune and the rebels extended their demand to other countries.

Switzerland, once again facing a moral dilemma on what to do with secret bank accounts of dictators, said it was still reviewing a request on Wednesday from the public prosecutor of the rebel-held city of Lubumbashi to freeze Mobutu funds.
The veteran strongman is sick with cancer and rebel forces are within striking distance of his capital, Kinshasa.
"The main priority is to establish whether the Zairean request is legitimate," government spokesman Achille Casanova told Reuters.
Switzerland has already ordered banks to hunt for the funds of Mobutu, estimated by the Swiss media at some $4 billion.
But banking sources said there may not be much money left in the secretive Swiss banks by the time the government makes up its mind. "We hear the money is just leaking out," said one.
Rebel representatives said the request from Zaire was legitimate because the Lubumbashi prosecutor had been appointed by Mobutu, although he later switched sides to join the rebels.
At a news conference, three exiled opponents of Mobutu representing the rebels, accompanied by a Swiss lawyer, produced evidence of the prosecutor's appointment in 1995 by Mobutu.
They said they handed the Berne government evidence of alleged corruption and embezzlement by Mobutu and accounts from witnesses, including the head of a Zairean mining company.

They also extended their demand to have Mobutu's assets frozen in the United States, France and Belgium, all former allies from the days when the West saw the Zairean leader as a bulwark against communism.
"Mobutu is still president, but the prosecutor of Lubumbashi is also a legitimate prosecutor," said Jose Mutombo-Kady, one of the exiles.
"Now it is official. We demand an urgent provisional blockage of funds to stop the money leaving Swiss banks. We believe all conditions for this demand are in place."
A top Swiss bank official told Reuters that he thought the government may go ahead with a decision to freeze Mobutu's assets.

"But I don't think there's much money. We've had clear signals from different sides for a long time that Mobutu as a bank client was risky business," said Georg Krayer, president of the Swiss Bankers Association.
It is not the first time Swiss banks have faced the problem of how to deal with the looted riches of dictators.

Protracted legal battles over the millions of late Philippine ruler Ferdinand Marcos are still going on. The ill-gotten gains of other toppled strongmen such as Haiti's Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier have also ended up in court.

Some Swiss fear that Mobutu's wealth will explode into another banking scandal -- the last thing Switzerland needs as it desperately tries to defend the nation's image amid recent scrutiny of its extensive wartime dealings with Nazi Germany.
Krayer warned the issue could explode into a "Marcos Two" if divided Zairean factions started fighting for the spoils.
"Now, it looks as if Mr Kabila is wearing a whiter hat than Mr Mobutu. But will he be head of state? Who is governing this country? This is tricky business," he said.
"The question is, if Mobutu falls, will factions fighting against him still be united? It could be that for three months we have no government in Zaire," Krayer said.
"In that case, we could have a Marcos Two. If it leads to that, than the outcome would be disputable."
